effect_estimate.comment: No inferential statistical effect estimate or regression is reported; quantitative results are descriptive CSR expenditure/project tabulations from the Odisha State CSR Portal, while household water and sanitation outcomes across the 264 sampled households are reported qualitatively in Tables 3 and 4.
effect_estimate.value: Descriptive quantitative and qualitative findings (no inferential numeric effect estimate reported): Across FY 2014-15 to 2019-20 under mandatory CSR (Companies Act 2013), Koraput received Rs. 14,369.82 lakh in CSR expenditure (5.2% of Odisha's total), including Rs. 2,161.19 lakh (15.0%) for Rural Development, Rs. 2,041.5 lakh (14.2%) for Swachh Bharat, Rs. 404.67 lakh earmarked for toilet construction, and Rs. 148.25 lakh invested in water service infrastructure; of 32 CSR rural development projects launched in Koraput, 53% were completed and 47% ongoing (41% implemented by State agencies, 31% by companies, 3% by NGOs, 25% anonymous). Qualitatively, compliance-driven CSR projects built physical structures without community consultation, needs/groundwater assessment, or maintenance: toilets constructed with poor quality or without piped water connections remained unused (used for storage or bypassed for open defecation, whereas Jhulaguda villagers used toilets paired with continuous stream-based piped water), and most CSR piped water systems, overhead tanks, and borewells/tubewells became dysfunctional, defunct, or choked with pollutants, leaving villagers reliant on unsafe river and stream water.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 6-16, Tables 2-4 and Graphs 1-5; PDF p. 17, Observations and Findings

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at 2 by the non-experimental mixed-methods design ceiling; rated 2 because field interviews, focus group discussions, direct observations, and CSR portal audits directly observe how compliance-driven CSR administration, fluid reporting heads, lack of community consultation, and absent maintenance/hydrogeological planning resulted in unused toilets and dysfunctional water infrastructure.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 11-17, Projects at a Glance, Tables 3-4, and Observations and Findings

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines mandatory CSR governance under the Companies Act 2013, including lack of feasibility, needs, and groundwater planning before construction (ELIGIBILITY: planning); corporate CSR discretion in fluidly classifying rural development expenditure heads and selectively targeting villages/beneficiaries (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION: discretion); unredressed community complaints to CSR officers and authorities regarding defunct/polluted infrastructure alongside weak monitoring and impact-assessment compliance (ENFORCEMENT: complaint); absence of beneficiary consultation and community ownership (participation); and fragmented multi-agency implementation and politically motivated CSR allocation across State agencies, corporations, and NGOs (institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, ENFORCEMENT, planning, discretion, complaint, participation, institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 4, 6, 9-10, 11-18, Tables 3-4 and Observations and Findings

outcome_flags.comment: Directly assesses CSR drinking water provision and infrastructure (water_access), household/school toilet construction and open defecation practices (sanitation_access), polluted/muddy water and pollutant-choked pipes versus safe potable/filtered water (service_quality), dysfunctional/malfunctioning/defunct borewells, tubewells, overhead tanks, and piped supply systems (service_reliability), and continuous/round-the-clock piped supply versus post-installation breakdown and seasonal summer drying (service_continuity).
outcome_flags.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 5, Research Objective, Data and Methodology; PDF pp. 11-16, Projects at a Glance and Tables 3-4

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: The study explicitly combines descriptive quantitative empirical analysis of CSR expenditure and project records (Tables 1-2, Graphs 1-5) with primary qualitative fieldwork (interviews, focus group discussions, and field observations across 264 randomly sampled beneficiary households in 8 villages; Tables 3-4), matching MMAT.
risk_of_bias_tool.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 5, Research Objective, Data and Methodology; PDF pp. 6-16, Result and Discussion

sample_size.comment: Multistage stratified sampling purposively selected 2 companies (HAL Koraput and NALCO Damanjodi) and 4 villages per company (8 villages total), then randomly selected 264 beneficiary households using the Yamane (1967) formula; supplemented with secondary CSR portal data covering 7 companies and 32 rural development projects in Koraput (2014-2020).
sample_size.value: 264 beneficiary households across 8 villages (4 villages each from 2 companies: HAL Koraput and NALCO Damanjodi); secondary CSR portal data covering 7 companies and 32 rural development projects (2014-2020)
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 5, Research Objective, Data and Methodology; PDF p. 9, Rural Development Projects in Koraput and the Role of Companies

study_design.comment: Authors describe relying on both quantitative and qualitative data from secondary and primary sources: descriptive quantitative compilation of Odisha State CSR Portal (Go Care) and company annual report expenditure/project data (2014-2020) combined with primary household interviews, focus group discussions, and field observations across 264 multistage stratified randomly sampled households analyzed qualitatively via the ASRSS framework and verbatim narratives.
study_design.value: Mixed-methods empirical study combining descriptive quantitative analysis of secondary CSR expenditure records (2014-2020) with primary qualitative interviews, focus group discussions, and field observations across multistage stratified randomly sampled households
